title: The Summer Plague: Polio
summary: For many years, summer was the scariest time of year for parents, because a sneaky virus called polio could paralyse children. Swimming pools closed, families fled the cities, and some patients needed a giant metal machine to help them breathe. Then three scientists in Boston learned how to grow the virus in a dish, and the race for a vaccine began.

sections.heading: A Virus That Usually Hides
paragraphs: Imagine it is July in an American town in the early 1950s. The air is hot and sticky, school is out, and you would love nothing more than a trip to the public swimming pool. But the pool has a sign on the gate: closed until further notice. The cinema is half empty. Your parents have told you not to drink from water fountains and not to play with children from the next street. Nobody says the word out loud very often, but everybody knows what they are afraid of. Polio.

Polio is short for poliomyelitis, a disease caused by a tiny virus called the poliovirus. The long name comes from Greek words: polios means grey, myelos means marrow, and the ending -itis means inflammation, or swelling and irritation. Put together, it means inflammation of the grey matter of the spinal cord, which is exactly the part of the body the virus can damage in its worst cases. In older books you will often see another name for it: infantile paralysis, because so many of its victims were small children.

The poliovirus does not usually travel through the air like a cold. Instead it lives and multiplies in the gut, the long tube of the intestines. An infected person sheds huge numbers of virus particles in their poo, sometimes for as long as six weeks. If even a tiny, invisible trace gets onto unwashed hands, toys, food or drinking water, the next person can swallow it. Scientists call this the faecal-oral route, which is a polite way of saying from poo to mouth. That is why clean water, good toilets and handwashing matter so much in the story of polio.

Here is the strange and important thing about polio: most people who catch it never know. Around seven in every ten infections cause no symptoms at all. About one in four causes a mild illness that looks like flu, with a sore throat, a slight fever or an upset tummy, and goes away within a week or two. A small number of people develop a stiff, painful neck and headache when the virus irritates the coverings of the brain and spinal cord, but they usually recover completely.

Only in a very small fraction of infections, fewer than one in a hundred and often far fewer, does the virus do its worst. In those cases it travels from the gut into the bloodstream and then along nerves into the spinal cord. There it attacks motor neurons, the long nerve cells that carry messages from the brain to the muscles telling them to move. When those nerve cells are destroyed, the muscles they controlled stop receiving any messages. They go floppy and weak, and over time they can waste away. This is called paralysis. Today the World Health Organization estimates that about one infection in every 200 leads to paralysis that does not go away, usually in the legs.

The most dangerous form is called bulbar polio, because it damages the brainstem, the part of the brain once called the bulb, which controls breathing and swallowing. If the muscles that fill the lungs with air are paralysed, a person can no longer breathe on their own. Before modern hospital machines, that often meant death. Even today, WHO estimates that between 5 and 10 in every 100 people who are paralysed by polio die because their breathing muscles stop working.

There are actually three slightly different types of poliovirus, called type 1, type 2 and type 3. Catching one type does not protect you against the other two, a fact that would make building a vaccine much harder. And because so many infected people show no symptoms at all, polio was a hidden enemy. For every child in hospital with a paralysed leg, there could be a hundred or more people walking around feeling perfectly well, quietly spreading the virus without knowing it.

sections.heading: An Old Disease with a New Pattern
paragraphs: Polio is not a new disease. A carved stone slab from ancient Egypt, made more than 3,000 years ago, shows a priest leaning on a staff, with one leg thin and shortened and his foot pointed downwards. Many doctors think he may have had polio, although nobody can be completely sure from a picture. Through the centuries, doctors occasionally described children who suddenly became lame after a fever. But for most of history, polio seems to have been an uncommon disease that appeared here and there, one child at a time.

That began to change in the 1800s. In 1840 a German doctor named Jakob Heine wrote a careful description of the disease and showed that the problem lay in the spinal cord. In 1890 a Swedish doctor, Karl Oskar Medin, studied a cluster of cases in Stockholm and realised that polio could strike many people at once, in an epidemic. Another Swede, Ivar Wickman, made a brilliant observation in the early 1900s: during an outbreak, children with only mild illness, or no obvious illness at all, were helping to spread it. Polio was more contagious than anyone had guessed.

Then came the first big outbreak in the United States. In the summer of 1894, in the Otter Creek valley around Rutland, Vermont, 132 people fell ill and 18 died. More and bigger summer epidemics followed in Europe and North America. In 1908 and 1909, an Austrian scientist named Karl Landsteiner, working in Vienna with Erwin Popper, took spinal cord tissue from a child who had died of polio, ground it up, passed it through a filter and injected it into monkeys. The monkeys became paralysed. Whatever caused polio was something that could pass through filters that stopped bacteria. It was a virus, even though nobody could yet see one.

So why did a disease that had been quietly present for thousands of years suddenly start exploding into epidemics just as cities were getting cleaner and healthier? It sounds backwards, but the leading explanation is that cleanliness itself changed the pattern of polio.

Think about life in a crowded town in, say, 1850. There was no clean piped water in many homes, few proper toilets and sewers, and plenty of dirt. Almost every baby would meet the poliovirus very early in life, often while still in nappies. At that age, babies still carry some protective antibodies that passed to them from their mothers before birth and through breast milk. Those borrowed antibodies helped keep the infection mild. The baby would then build its own lifelong immunity, almost always without anyone noticing.

By the late 1800s and early 1900s, wealthy countries were building sewers, filtering drinking water and teaching handwashing. These changes saved enormous numbers of lives from diseases such as cholera and typhoid. But they also meant that many children now met the poliovirus later, at age three, five, ten or even as teenagers or adults. By then the protection from their mothers had faded away, and an older child or adult is more likely to suffer paralysis than a baby. Most historians and scientists accept this explanation, although they still debate the details, such as exactly how much each factor mattered.

One clue supports the idea: polio epidemics often hit comfortable, clean neighbourhoods hard, sometimes harder than poor and crowded ones. That surprised people at the time, who were used to thinking of epidemics as diseases of dirt and poverty. Polio was different. It was, in a strange way, a disease of modern life.

sections.heading: The Terrible Summer of 1916
paragraphs: In June 1916, doctors in Brooklyn, New York, noticed that more and more young children were becoming paralysed. On 17 June the city's health department officially announced an epidemic. Over the following weeks, cases climbed steeply, peaking in early August. It became the worst polio epidemic the world had yet seen.

By the end of the year, New York City alone had recorded about 9,000 cases and more than 2,000 deaths. Across the United States there were about 27,000 cases and more than 6,000 deaths. The youngest children were hit hardest: in New York, children aged one to three made up a large share of cases, and most of the children who died were under five.

Nobody knew how polio spread, so health officials tried almost everything they could think of. Homes with a sick child had a printed warning card, called a placard, nailed beside the door, and families were kept inside under quarantine. Newspapers printed the names and addresses of patients each day. Cinemas and public gatherings were restricted, children under 16 were kept away from many public places, and parents were warned to keep their children away from swimming pools, beaches, fountains and amusement parks.

Fear also led people to wrong guesses. Some blamed flies, so cities cracked down on horse manure where flies bred. Some blamed sewers, or car exhaust. Many people believed pets spread polio, and tens of thousands of cats were killed in New York that summer, all for nothing, because cats do not carry human poliovirus. Some people unfairly blamed immigrant families, especially Italian Americans, and Black Americans, even though the disease struck every kind of neighbourhood. Staten Island, the part of the city with the fewest immigrants, actually had the highest proportion of cases.

Families who could afford it fled. The New York Times estimated that by early July around 50,000 children had been sent out of the city to the countryside and mountains. Some nearby towns posted police at train stations and ferry docks to turn back travellers from New York. In the city, some frightened mothers sealed the cracks around their windows with rags in the summer heat, hoping to keep the disease out.

The 1916 epidemic taught Americans to fear summer. Polio would return again and again over the next four decades, usually starting in late spring and reaching its peak in July, August and September. It is not fully clear why polio loved summer so much, although warm weather may help the virus survive longer outside the body, and children spend more time swimming and playing together. Whatever the reason, the phrase summer plague stuck. Every year, parents watched the newspapers for reports of the first cases, and every year some children who had gone happily to camp in June came home in braces, on crutches or in wheelchairs.

sections.heading: A Future President Falls Ill
paragraphs: Polio did not only strike children. In August 1921, a tall, energetic 39-year-old politician named Franklin Delano Roosevelt was on holiday with his family at their summer house on Campobello Island, just across the border from Maine in Canada. Roosevelt had already been the Assistant Secretary of the Navy and had run, unsuccessfully, for Vice President of the United States the year before. He was famous for his sailing, swimming and boundless energy.

On 10 August, after a tiring day outdoors, he went to bed feeling chilled and achy. Over the next few days things became much worse. He had a fever, and weakness crept upwards through his body until he could not stand. His legs became paralysed. On 25 August a well-known specialist, Dr Robert Lovett, examined him and declared that it was clearly poliomyelitis. Most of his other symptoms faded over the following months, but Roosevelt never walked unaided again. He was paralysed from the waist down for the rest of his life.

Was it really polio? In 2003 a team of researchers led by Armond Goldman looked again at the descriptions of Roosevelt's illness. They pointed out that some details, such as his age, the way the paralysis climbed upwards and spread evenly on both sides, his facial weakness and the numbness and painful sensitivity of his skin, fit better with a different illness called Guillain-Barré syndrome, in which the body's own immune system attacks the nerves. Other doctors have argued back that polio is still the best explanation. Nobody can test Roosevelt now, so the question may never be settled. What is certain is that Roosevelt himself, his doctors and the whole country believed he had polio, and that belief shaped history.

Roosevelt refused to let paralysis end his career. He worked for years to strengthen his body, learning to stand with heavy metal braces on his legs and to walk short distances while gripping a cane and someone's arm. In 1924 he visited Warm Springs, Georgia, where a natural spring fed a pool of warm water, and found that swimming in it helped him exercise. In 1926 he bought the resort and turned it into a treatment centre for polio patients, where people could exercise, swim and support one another.

In 1928 he was elected Governor of New York, and in 1932 he was elected President of the United States. He went on to win four presidential elections, more than anyone else in American history, and led the country through the Great Depression and most of the Second World War. Yet many Americans never fully realised how disabled he was. Photographers mostly agreed not to take pictures of him being lifted or using his wheelchair, his speeches were arranged so he could grip a sturdy lectern, and he usually appeared in public standing, holding the arm of an aide or one of his sons. Roosevelt hid his disability partly because in the 1920s and 1930s many people wrongly believed that a disabled person could not be a strong leader.

sections.heading: Marching with Dimes
paragraphs: Roosevelt could not hide from polio itself, though, and he decided to fight it. On 3 January 1938 he founded the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, a charity that would pay for patient care and, crucially, for scientific research. His old law partner and friend Basil O'Connor ran it, and he kept leading it for more than thirty years, building a network of over 3,000 local chapters across the country.

The foundation's genius was asking for tiny amounts of money from enormous numbers of people. The popular entertainer Eddie Cantor suggested on the radio that every American could send a dime, a ten-cent coin, to the President. He called the campaign the March of Dimes, a joke on a famous cinema newsreel of the time called The March of Time. The idea caught on wildly. Envelopes poured into the White House, some with a single coin taped to a card. By the final count, about 2,680,000 dimes arrived, worth 268,000 dollars, and the newspapers joked about a silver tide swamping the White House mail room. The charity later took March of Dimes as its official name.

Every January, around Roosevelt's birthday on the 30th, the campaign returned. Cinemas passed collection cans along the rows. Children collected coins at school. In 1950, mothers in Phoenix, Arizona, came up with the Mothers' March on Polio: on a chosen evening, porch lights were switched on as a signal, and volunteer mothers walked from door to door collecting donations. The idea spread across the country. Posters showed brave poster children in leg braces; the first, Donald Anderson of Oregon, had caught polio in 1943.

The money did two big jobs. First, it paid for care: hospital beds, braces, wheelchairs, physiotherapy and iron lungs, so that families did not have to face ruinous bills alone. Second, and most important for our story, it paid for research. Many of the scientists you will meet in this part and the next were funded by ordinary people's dimes. After Roosevelt died in April 1945, the US government honoured him by putting his face on the dime, first issued on 30 January 1946, his birthday. It is still on the dime today.

sections.heading: The Machine That Breathed
paragraphs: For the children with bulbar polio, whose breathing muscles stopped working, the danger was immediate. Without help they would slowly suffocate. In 1928 two researchers at the Harvard School of Public Health, the engineer Philip Drinker and the physiologist Louis Agassiz Shaw Jr., built a machine to breathe for them. It became known as the iron lung.

The iron lung was a large metal tank, roughly the size and shape of a small submarine, with the patient lying inside on a bed and only their head sticking out through a tight rubber collar at one end. Here is how it worked. Normally, when you breathe in, muscles pull your chest outwards. That makes a little more space inside your lungs, the air pressure inside them drops slightly, and outside air rushes in to fill the gap. The iron lung did the same job from the outside. A pump sucked some air out of the sealed tank, lowering the pressure around the patient's body. The chest expanded and air flowed in through the nose and mouth. Then the pressure in the tank rose back up, the chest sank down again, and air flowed out. Doctors call this negative-pressure ventilation.

Drinker and Shaw's first prototype used an electric motor and air pumps taken from two vacuum cleaners. On 12 October 1928, at Boston Children's Hospital, it was tried on an eight-year-old girl who was close to death because polio had stopped her breathing. Within moments of the pump starting, she was breathing again. The story of that first rescue helped make the iron lung famous.

The early machines were expensive. In 1930 an adult Drinker respirator cost about 2,000 dollars, a huge sum at the time, more than many families earned in a year. In 1931 an inventor named John Haven Emerson introduced an improved, cheaper version with a bed that slid in and out and windows in the side so nurses could reach in to adjust the patient. In Britain, a cheaper wooden version designed by Edward Both was produced in large numbers in the late 1930s with funding from the businessman Lord Nuffield.

During the great epidemics of the 1940s and 1950s, hospitals set up whole wards filled with rows of iron lungs, their pumps wheezing in rhythm day and night. Nurses fed patients, read to them and held up mirrors so they could see the room behind them. Many patients needed the machine for only a week or two until their breathing muscles recovered enough to work on their own. But some were left permanently paralysed and lived in iron lungs for years. The American Paul Alexander caught polio in 1952 at the age of six and used an iron lung for the rest of his life; despite this, he learned to breathe on his own for periods by gulping air, earned a law degree, worked as a lawyer and wrote a book. He died in 2024 at age 78, after 72 years in the machine.

In 1952 a terrible epidemic in Copenhagen, Denmark, overwhelmed the city's few respirators. The doctors, guided by the anaesthetist Bjørn Ibsen, tried a different approach: they placed a tube into the patient's windpipe and pushed air gently into the lungs with a squeezable bag. Because there were no machines to do it, hundreds of medical students took turns squeezing bags by hand, around the clock, for weeks. Death rates among patients with breathing paralysis fell dramatically. This positive-pressure method soon replaced the iron lung in most hospitals, and it was the beginning of the modern intensive care unit.

sections.heading: Growing a Virus in a Dish
paragraphs: Iron lungs saved lives, but they did not stop anyone from catching polio. To do that, scientists needed a vaccine. And to make a vaccine, they first needed to grow huge amounts of poliovirus. That was a big problem.

Remember that a virus cannot copy itself on its own. It has to get inside living cells and hijack them. For decades the only reliable way to grow poliovirus was inside the brains and spinal cords of living monkeys. That was slow, enormously expensive and used vast numbers of animals. Worse, vaccine made from nerve tissue carried a risk of causing dangerous allergic reactions in the brain. Many scientists believed poliovirus could only grow in nerve cells, so they saw no way around the problem.

At Boston Children's Hospital, a calm, careful virologist named John Enders was working with two young doctors, Thomas Weller and Frederick Robbins, on growing other viruses in tubes of living tissue kept alive in a nourishing liquid. Newly available antibiotics, such as penicillin and streptomycin, helped them keep their tissue cultures free of the bacteria that had so often ruined such experiments in the past. In 1948 they had some poliovirus sitting in the lab freezer, and they decided to try putting it into tubes of human tissue that was not nerve tissue at all.

To almost everyone's surprise, the virus grew. They could even see the effect under a microscope: the cells in infected tubes became damaged and died, while cells in uninfected tubes stayed healthy. That gave scientists a way to tell whether live virus was present in a sample, and whether a person's blood contained antibodies that could block it, all without using a single monkey for the test. Enders, Weller and Robbins published their discovery in the journal Science in January 1949.

It is hard to overstate how important this was. Now poliovirus could be grown in large quantities in flasks of cells, such as cells from monkey kidneys, instead of in the nervous systems of living animals. The method, called tissue culture or cell culture, became one of the basic tools of modern virology, and it is still used to make many vaccines today. In 1954 the three men shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and Enders is sometimes called the father of modern vaccines.

The new tool arrived just in time, because polio was getting worse, not better. The year 1952 brought the worst polio epidemic in American history: 57,628 reported cases, 3,145 deaths and more than 21,000 people left with some degree of paralysis. Parents who had grown up during the 1916 epidemic now watched their own children face an even bigger one. The pressure on scientists to find a vaccine had never been greater.

Two researchers in particular were determined to be first. In Pittsburgh, a young scientist named Jonas Salk believed the safest approach was to kill the virus completely and inject it, so the immune system could learn its shape without any risk of infection. In Cincinnati, an older, sharp-tongued researcher named Albert Sabin was sure that only a live but weakened virus, swallowed by mouth, would give strong, long-lasting protection. Both men were brilliant, both were stubborn, and they disagreed with each other loudly. The race between their two very different ideas was about to begin.

deepDive: Why did polio become epidemic just as public health improved? The most widely accepted answer is often called the hygiene or delayed-exposure explanation. In places with poor sanitation, nearly every child is infected with poliovirus in the first year or two of life, while still partly protected by maternal antibodies passed across the placenta and in breast milk. Paralysis is rarer in infants than in older children and adults, so infection in infancy produces widespread immunity with relatively little visible disease. When sanitation improves, the average age of first infection rises, maternal protection is gone, and the proportion of infections that lead to paralysis climbs. Supporting evidence includes the observation that early 20th-century epidemics in the US and Scandinavia often hit better-off families hard, and that the age of polio patients rose over the first half of the century, with more cases among older children, teenagers and adults by the 1940s and 1950s. Historians caution that other factors may also have mattered, including changes in virus strains, better reporting and diagnosis, and population growth in cities, so the hygiene explanation is the leading account rather than the whole story. The numbers themselves need care too. Reported case counts from the early 1900s mostly reflect paralytic cases that doctors noticed, while the true number of infections was hundreds of times higher because most were silent. Figures for the 1916 epidemic differ slightly between sources: about 27,000 US cases and somewhere between 6,000 and 7,000 deaths, with over 2,000 deaths in New York City. Roosevelt's diagnosis is another live debate. A 2003 analysis in the Journal of Medical Biography used his symptoms and Bayesian reasoning to argue that Guillain-Barré syndrome was more likely; critics replied that the evidence is incomplete and polio remains plausible. Finally, the iron lung story shows how technology and epidemics shape each other: the 1952 Copenhagen epidemic, where death rates among patients with breathing paralysis fell sharply after the switch to tube-and-bag positive-pressure ventilation, is widely seen as the birth of intensive care medicine.
funFact: When Drinker and Shaw built their first iron lung prototype in 1928, they powered it with air pumps borrowed from two vacuum cleaners.

check.q: What breakthrough did John Enders, Thomas Weller and Frederick Robbins announce in 1949 that made a polio vaccine possible?
check.a: They grew poliovirus in tubes of human tissue that was not nerve tissue
wrong: They invented the iron lung to help paralysed patients breathe
They proved that cats and flies spread polio
They photographed the poliovirus with an ordinary light microscope
